issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For a police trauma profile, the trigger set is not clinically coherent as a group. Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. It more commonly fits sexual assault or severe physical violation. Here it is unsupported by the trigger and memory items, which focus on fragmented recall and guilt rather than shame/violation themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance towards dangerous people could occur after police trauma, but in this profile it is weakly supported because the triggers point toward accident/fire cues rather than interpersonal threat cues. This creates a cross-node mismatch between maladaptive strategy content and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette:
Ravi, a 41-year-old South Asian graphic designer, came to treatment after nearly a year of living as though ordinary life had become a series of hidden ambushes. The trauma that still organized his days began on an evening walk home from the train station, when he was stopped by police officers responding to a report of a suspicious man in the area. He had trusted the uniformed officer who asked to see his identification, relieved to comply and eager to be cooperative, but the encounter turned abruptly when he was searched, pushed against a wall, and left humiliated and confused as bystanders watched. What stayed with him most was not only the physical force but the smell of something burnt from a nearby alley—an oily, acrid odor that seemed to attach itself to the scene. Since then, the smell of burnt food, burnt toast, or even a scorched electrical cord could drag him back to that night with startling force, and the sight of police, security guards, or any person in uniform had the same effect. When those cues appeared, he would feel the event return in fragments rather than as a coherent story: he knew what happened, but when he tried to describe it, the words would not come, and the account would slip away before he could finish.

Ravi had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that the world was a dangerous place, and that he had been betrayed by someone he had once believed was there to protect him. Those beliefs shaped the meaning of the memory every time it surfaced. He did not remember the encounter as a single bad night; he remembered it as proof that authority could turn on him without warning, and that being reasonable or compliant offered no protection. The more he returned to that interpretation, the more the memory filled with shame and self-reproach. He would remember the officer’s face, the shouting, the moment his hands were forced behind him, and then be overwhelmed by intense guilt, as if he should have done something different, said the right thing, or recognized the danger sooner. He found himself unable to find words for it, and when he tried to tell his wife or a colleague, he lost the thread halfway through and stopped, frustrated and embarrassed by his own silence.

In the months that followed, Ravi began rehearsing conversations before almost any interaction. He would stand in the kitchen before answering the phone, practicing what to say if a neighbor asked a question, or if someone in the lobby stopped him, or if a parking attendant challenged him. At work as a graphic designer, even a routine email from a client could send him into careful mental scripting before he replied, as though the wrong phrase might expose him to someone dangerous. That effort to stay prepared kept his attention fixed on what might go wrong, and he became increasingly vigilant for dangerous people wherever he went, scanning faces, hands, badges, and body language in the office building, on the train, and outside the grocery store. Because he was constantly anticipating threat, the presence of uniforms and the smell of burnt food became even more charged; he noticed them immediately, and each sight or odor seemed to pull the memory back into the present before he had time to think.

His attempts to manage the fear gradually hardened the beliefs that had begun the cycle. The more Ravi rehearsed and controlled his speech, the more convinced he became that people were untrustworthy and that the safest assumption was danger. Avoiding future plans followed naturally from that outlook. He stopped agreeing to trips, deferred family outings, and would not commit to projects at work that extended beyond the week, telling himself that planning ahead only set him up for disappointment or exposure. Even his marriage narrowed around his caution; his wife noticed how often he asked what would happen next and how little he would say about weekends or holidays. Yet despite all this preparation, he still felt ambushed by the cues he could not fully control. A burnt smell drifting from a neighboring apartment, a police car passing his building, a uniformed maintenance worker in the lobby—each could bring the scene back and leave him shaken, mute, and ashamed, which in turn sent him back into more rehearsing and more scanning.

By the time he sought help, Ravi was exhausted by the effort of keeping himself ready for danger and by the loneliness of carrying a memory he could not explain. What finally brought him in was a recent evening when he smelled something burnt in the hallway of his apartment building and saw two police officers speaking with a tenant downstairs; he froze, could not speak when his wife asked what was wrong, and spent the rest of the night pacing and checking the locks. He said he was most afraid that he would spend the rest of his life expecting betrayal from every authority figure and every unfamiliar face, but he was also hoping to find a way to speak about what happened without losing the thread, and to stop living as if the next burnt smell or uniform meant the same thing would happen again.
